prize_parts.citation: for discoveries on the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B033 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case rests on the science. It is a complete arc from proglucagon processing and incretin physiology, through the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its insulinotropic and intestinotropic actions, to agonists whose effects on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes have been confirmed in independent large trials. Maturity is not in question, and the citation can be stated in one sentence. The round-1 exchange tested the configuration and did not weaken it. All six members converged on the same three names and the same stated weaknesses, but I do not count that as an argument. What persuades me is that two of the three names, Holst and Drucker, are secure under any resolution of the priority questions. The only contested slot is the third one, and the contest concerns who identified the active form. It does not concern the discovery itself.
statement.case_against: The third name remains exposed. Mojsov's priority for the active truncated peptide is contested, early proglucagon investigators such as Habener are outside the supplied credit list, and Knudsen, who led liraglutide and semaglutide, is excluded by the three-person cap. None of us can audit that record from the supplied material, and I am still working from recollection. If the committee judges the active-peptide priority unsettled, the honest options are narrow. We can name Drucker and Holst only, or we can replace Mojsov with Knudsen and change the prize from discovery to development. I would prefer the first, because the second turns the third slot into a different argument. A further risk is that a prize crediting only the physiology will be read as passing over the people who made the medicine. I accept that cost and do not think it justifies removing a discovery scientist.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps Mojsov in the trio while admitting he cannot audit the priority record, and treats Hall plus Schreiber as the cleaner TOR core, with B039 and B004 as later or second-part candidates.
responses.response: We agree that the unresolved name is a reason to examine the allocation and not a reason to prefer a candidate with a cleaner trio but less impact. I would go one step further than in round 1. Because none of us can verify the GLP-1(7-36) record from the supplied files, I think the committee should decide in advance what it does if the record cannot be settled. My answer is that the prize does not fall and does not drift to a development configuration. It becomes Drucker and Holst with an appropriately worded citation, and I would accept that over naming someone I cannot defend. I also welcome your revision on TOR, since it removes a competitor for the second-part question without any need to argue the point further.

responses.point: Sandberg calls Mojsov the weakest link but keeps her, wants the citation to make the therapeutic consequence visible, and says that if the committee wants the drug rewarded the answer is a different configuration and not a quiet name substitution.
responses.response: I agree with the last point and I support it. A substitution of Knudsen for Mojsov should be argued openly as a choice to reward development, not slipped in as a repair of the third slot. I also support your wording suggestion. The citation I propose says that the discoveries made incretin-based treatment possible, so the therapeutic consequence is visible without crediting the development step itself. Where I would push back is on your remark that Mojsov's identification of the active form is what made the concept coherent. I think that is true, but it is the thing we cannot audit. It is a stronger reason to keep her only if the priority record bears it out. If it does not, I would not keep her on the strength of the narrative.

responses.point: Linnarsson thinks the CAR-T prize is better as June and Sadelain, calls Rosenberg's work adoptive cell therapy more broadly than the CAR construct, and says he would not oppose a compact two-person TNF prize.
responses.response: I have reconsidered Rosenberg in light of your argument and Sandberg's, and I now hold the view with less confidence than before. His adoptive transfer and first gene-engineered T-cell trials gave the clinical precedent, but the discovery the prize would name is the engineered receptor, and Eshhar's absence is the larger gap whichever way we go. I therefore still list B039 as my first alternative, not as a competitor to B033. On TNF I take your point that it validated a cytokine as a target in an established disease, while CAR-T created a new class of treatment. That difference in novelty of principle is a fair reason to put B036 behind B039, and my alternatives order already reflects it. I do not claim B036 should win a second part this year.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the committee can settle the third slot and whether the citation should stress physiology or the therapeutic consequence, and says he did not rank B036 in his top eight.
responses.response: My answer to your first question is that the supplied evidence cannot settle the third slot, so the fallback has to be agreed now. That fallback is Drucker and Holst, as I said to Perlmann. On the citation, I propose the discovery wording with the therapeutic consequence stated in its closing clause, and I do not want Knudsen's work recognised inside the prize at the cost of a discovery name. On a second part, I do not support one. The GLP-1 part already uses all three names and a second part would give no clear gain. I take your reservation about B036 as fair. I ranked it second as a clean bench-to-bedside case, but I accept that the antibody engineers and TNF biologists outside the pair make it read as translational, and I do not argue it should displace B039.

responses.point: El-Manira would test a Holst and Drucker pair before deciding on Mojsov, and would put TNF blockade behind CAR-T in any two-part prize.
responses.response: I support testing the pair. The case for B033 is not reduced if the committee finds the active-peptide priority too uncertain for Mojsov. Holst's work on secretion and incretin action in humans and Drucker's work on receptor biology and the therapeutic rationale carry the physiology. What is lost is the identification of the active peptide, and the citation can still refer to its active form only if that record supports it. I also accept your ordering of B039 ahead of B036 for a two-part prize. Since no member prefers two parts, I do not think the committee needs to decide that ordering this year.

uncertainties: Priority for identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and whether Habener or other early contributors outside the supplied list should come ahead of Mojsov. I cannot resolve this from the supplied material.
Whether the committee will accept a two-name fallback of Drucker and Holst if the third slot cannot be defended, and whether the citation can then still refer to the active form.
Whether the committee wants the prize to reach the drugs, which would require a separate, openly argued configuration involving Knudsen.
Eshhar's missing role in B039, and whether B036 is a primary discovery or a translation of earlier cytokine and antibody work.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B033, and I have found nothing new in round 1 that changes that. My field of autoimmunity and rheumatology is adjacent to B036 (TNF blockade) and B039 (CAR-T), which are my alternatives and not my preferred configuration. My profile documents no personal or institutional connection to Feldmann, Maini, June, Sadelain, Rosenberg or any of the B033 names, so this is topical proximity only. I would recuse if a documented tie to a credited individual appeared.
